units.en: For the buying and selling of ⟦0⟧ with ⟦1⟧, see ⟦2⟧.
⟦0⟧ is the exchange of goods between countries, consisting of ⟦1⟧ being exchanged for the use of ⟦2⟧.

Depending primarily on a country's ⟦0⟧, a percentage of its domestic strategic ⟦1⟧ extraction is set aside to be exported to the global market. These resources are unavailable for use by the producing country, regardless of whether trade deals have been struck for those resources or not. This mechanism is used to abstract a varying production level of resources. ⟦2⟧ can have additional access to their ⟦3⟧' resources beyond what would be dictated by their ⟦4⟧.

If a specific resource has no buyer, then it will not be exploited, and it will remain available to the market as untapped capacity. Resources can be bought with the production capacity generated by ⟦0⟧, meaning the resource-producing nation will receive ⟦1⟧ in exchange for their exported resources.

This has major implications for economic strategy and military planning. Since the portion of resource extraction capacity devoted to export is determined by the country's ⟦0⟧, having the right laws in effect can be critical. Ideally, a country wishes to keep exactly enough resources to satisfy its domestic ⟦1⟧ needs and export the rest to foreign buyers. In practice, this can be very difficult, and so countries may often want to seek out long-term trade partners with whom they can form mutualistic relationships, buying each other's resources that they can afford thanks to the factories received from each other's trade. Alternatively, countries can seek to create ⟦2⟧ whose resources they can then buy at a discount.

A country can conclude a trade deal with any non-hostile country with whom they have at least 0⟦0⟧ trade influence, to whom they have trade access, and who have goods available for export. The exporter does not need to approve of the deal and will not be notified that a deal has been made.

The importer will need to spend the production of at least 1 ⟦0⟧ as the cost of importing. Each ⟦1⟧ spent will allow the importation of a maximum of 8 units of a resource,⟦2⟧ if available on the market. Even if the exporting country is unable to export 8 units of a resource, the importing country will still need to spend the full ⟦3⟧ to strike the deal for whatever is left.

When importing goods from its ⟦0⟧, a country can buy more resources per ⟦1⟧. Closely aligned ⟦2⟧, such as ⟦3⟧ and ⟦4⟧, can offer huge discounts of 80 units of the resource per ⟦5⟧, while more independent ones, such as ⟦6⟧ and ⟦7⟧, offer more modest ones of between 16 and 10 resoures per factory.
Certain ⟦0⟧ can also enable special ⟦1⟧ or ⟦2⟧ that directly modify the number of resources that can be bought per ⟦3⟧. Examples include ⟦4⟧ for ⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧ for ⟦7⟧, and ⟦8⟧ for ⟦9⟧.

The ⟦0⟧ spent to purchase a country's ⟦1⟧ will be added to those of the exporter while the trade is ongoing. This means they will be available for ⟦2⟧, count for any ⟦3⟧ that require a certain amount of factories, and can be used to pay for various special projects, like those related to special ⟦4⟧ or ⟦5⟧. They can also be used to buy ⟦6⟧ from other countries, though this was not the case in earlier versions of the game.
Trade deals are automatically voided if the importer ceases to have enough ⟦0⟧ available to maintain them.

Even if a trade deal is made to buy a country's resources, those resources need to actually be able to be transported from the exporter to the importer for them to become available to the importer. For trade routes over land, this means that there needs to be a route through non-hostile countries through which the imported resources can be transported. For trade routes over the sea, the importing country needs to be able to allocate enough ⟦0⟧ to the trade route and to have valid ⟦1⟧ to the exporting country. Should no valid trade route become available to a given exporter, any active trade deals with said exporter will stop providing resources (though ⟦2⟧ will still be spent), and no new trade deals can be struck with the exporter.

When there is greater demand to buy a country's resources than what the country can produce, the tie breaker for who ends up being able to import how many resources is determined by the share of each potential importer's trade influence with the exporter.

If all potential importers' trade influence with the exporter is identical, then they can will be able to access equal shares of the exporter's resources. However, if one country has far more trade influence with the exporter than others, it will be able to access a far greater share of the exporters. Similarly, if a country has far less trade influence with the exporter than others, its maximum potential share of the exporter's exported resources will be far lower. For example, if one country has 120 trade influence with an exporter and another has only 80, in a scenario where there is not enough resources to satisfy the trade desires of both countries, the first country gets priority access for up to 60% of the exporter's resources, potentially being able to muscle out the second country's trade down to 40% of the exporter's resources. If then a third country enters the picture with 200 trade influence, then they get priority access to up to 50% of the exporter's resources to match their share of the total amount of trade influence competing for a resource, dropping the priority access shares of the first and second countries to 30% and 20%, respectively.
If trade influence reaches 0,⟦0⟧ a country may no longer import resources from the country in question. This typically only tends to happen through ⟦1⟧, though it can also happen through other means.
Trade influence is influenced by the following:
⟦0⟧ of the importing country with the exporting one: between ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧ scaling with ⟦4⟧
Distance between the two countries' capitals: ⟦0⟧ per 7.114 km⟦1⟧ of distance
Existing active trade deals: ⟦0⟧ per month, up to a maximum of ⟦1⟧
Support for the importing country's ruling ⟦0⟧ in the exporting country: up to ⟦1⟧ at 100% support
"Anti-monopoly" factor: ⟦0⟧ if the exporting country is selling at least 50%⟦1⟧ of their available resources to the importer
⟦0⟧ performing ⟦1⟧ mission: ⟦2⟧ per day (with a stacking ⟦3⟧ multiplier for each operative beyond the first), up to a maximum of ⟦4⟧

In practice, due to the relative scarcity of both ⟦0⟧ with which to buy ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ to consume those resources, the strategic importance of large resources deposits and wars in general will make trade influence usually irrelevant for the first few years of gameplay in any scenario. As the game progresses, however, trade influence can become a way to deny enemies access to vital resources from neutral countries.
